title: How to Use Chopsticks in Japan — and What Never to Do
excerpt: Using chopsticks correctly in Japan is less about technique and more about knowing the four things that are genuinely offensive. The technique is optional. The four things are not.

title: The Rules of Gift Giving in Japan: What to Give, How to Give It, When Not To
excerpt: Gift giving in Japan is governed by a set of conventions that are invisible until you get them wrong. Here is what they are.

title: Tattoos and Onsen in Japan: What the Policy Actually Is
excerpt: Most onsen ban tattoos. Fewer than you'd think actually enforce it. Here is how to navigate it honestly.

title: Meishi: The Japanese Business Card Ritual and Why It Matters
excerpt: In Japan, the business card is not a piece of paper. It is a physical representation of the person. Treating it as stationary is the fastest way to start a professional relationship poorly.

title: How to Order and Drink Sake in Japan Without Getting It Wrong
excerpt: Sake is Japan's most misunderstood drink. Most people drink it too warm, in the wrong glass, with the wrong food. This is how to do it correctly.

title: The Japanese Breakfast: What It Is and Why It Will Change Your Morning
excerpt: A traditional Japanese breakfast is not a quick meal. It is a composed sequence of small things done well, and eating it once will make every hotel breakfast you eat for the rest of your life feel like a concession.

title: The Best Time to Visit Japan: An Honest Month-by-Month Guide
excerpt: Spring cherry blossoms and autumn foliage are spectacular. They are also the two most crowded periods of the year. Here is what every month actually offers.

title: Taking a Taxi in Japan: What to Know Before You Get In
excerpt: Japanese taxis are expensive, exceptionally clean, and almost entirely driven by people who know exactly where they are going. The main things to know are not about navigation.

title: Matsumoto: The Castle Town That Gets Everything Right
excerpt: Two and a half hours from Tokyo, a city with one of Japan's three great original castles, a mountain backdrop, an excellent food scene, and a fraction of Kyoto's visitor numbers. There is no explanation for why more people don't come here.

title: Kyoto in Three Days: What to Actually See and What to Skip
excerpt: Kyoto has over 1,600 temples and shrines. You will not see them all. Here is how to choose the ones that matter — and what makes them worth choosing over the others.

title: The Unwritten Rules of Japanese Trains — Read This Before You Board
excerpt: Japan’s trains run on time to the minute and operate on a set of social rules that nobody posts on a sign. Here’s what they are.

title: How to Visit a Japanese Temple or Shrine Without Being Accidentally Rude
excerpt: Temples and shrines have different rules, different purposes, and different gods. Getting them confused is the starting mistake. Everything else follows from there.

title: Why You Should Never Tip in Japan — and What to Do Instead
excerpt: In Japan, the service is built into the price. Adding a tip doesn’t reward the server — it creates an awkward situation for both of you.

title: When to Take Your Shoes Off in Japan: The Complete Guide
excerpt: The shoe rule in Japan is not arbitrary. It reflects a clear line between outside space and inside space that structures daily life. Here is where that line is drawn.

title: How to Behave in Public in Japan: The Unwritten Rules
excerpt: Japanese public spaces operate on a set of unspoken rules that make them exceptionally pleasant. Most visitors don’t know them. All of them are learnable in ten minutes.

title: Japan Still Runs on Cash — Here’s How Much to Bring and Where to Get It
excerpt: Cards are increasingly accepted in Japan, but ‘increasingly’ is not the same as ‘reliably.’ Plan for cash and treat the card acceptance as a bonus.

title: SIM Card vs Pocket Wi-Fi in Japan: What Nobody Tells You Before You Choose
excerpt: Both work. One is significantly more convenient. The answer has changed in the last three years and most travel articles haven’t caught up.

title: The Only Japanese Phrases You Actually Need
excerpt: Japanese is difficult. A handful of phrases isn’t. The ten expressions below will handle the majority of situations a visitor encounters, and they take about 20 minutes to learn.

title: The Tokyo Subway: How to Navigate It Without Getting Lost
excerpt: Tokyo’s train network is the most complex urban rail system in the world. It is also, once you understand the basics, extremely easy to use.

title: What You Can and Cannot Photograph in Japan
excerpt: Japan is exceptionally photogenic. It also has specific places and situations where photography is restricted, disrespectful, or now actively prohibited. Knowing the difference matters.

title: Your First Ryokan: What to Expect, What to Do, and What Not to Wear
excerpt: A traditional Japanese inn is not a hotel. The sooner you accept that, the better the stay.

title: Why January Is the Best Month to Visit Japan (Yes, Really)
excerpt: No cherry blossoms. No 38-degree humidity. No crowds. January is when Japan stops performing for tourists and just exists.

title: The Convenience Store Is Japan's Greatest Culinary Achievement
excerpt: Seven-Eleven in Japan is not Seven-Eleven anywhere else. This distinction matters and deserves your full attention.

title: Tokyo's Kissaten: The Coffee Shops That Refuse to Change
excerpt: Somewhere between the third-wave cafés and the chain stores, Tokyo's old coffee shops have been quietly waiting.

title: Kanazawa: The City Most Japan Itineraries Skip — and Shouldn't
excerpt: Three hours from Tokyo by bullet train. A fraction of Kyoto's crowds. Arguably better seafood. There is no good reason it's on so few itineraries.

title: Tsukiji Outer Market: Where to Actually Eat (and What to Skip)
excerpt: The inner market moved to Toyosu in 2018. The outer market never moved and never needed to.

title: How to Eat at an Izakaya Without Looking Completely Lost
excerpt: The curtain over the door. The laminated menu with pictures on maybe two pages. The small charge you didn't order. You'll be fine.

title: The IC Card Is the Best Thing in Japan. Here's How to Actually Use It.
excerpt: You can survive Tokyo's train network without one. You just won't want to.

title: Japanese Whisky: What's Worth Buying and What's Just Marketing
excerpt: The golden age is over but the whisky is still exceptional. You just need to know what you're actually looking at.

title: Naoshima Is Japan's Art Island — and Nobody Tells You How to Do It Right
excerpt: It's a real island with real people living on it. The art just happens to be everywhere.

title: The JR Pass: Who It's For, Who It Isn't, and How to Not Overpay
excerpt: The JR Pass is one of Japan's most famous travel products. Since the 2023 price rise it is also, for most itineraries, a waste of money.

title: Where to Stay in Tokyo: Honest Assessments of Each Neighborhood
excerpt: Every first-time visitor books Shinjuku because someone told them to. Some of those people are right.

title: Japan's Four Major Ramen Styles: What They Are and Where to Actually Eat Them
excerpt: Ramen in Japan is not one food. Depending on where you are, the word covers a range of things that share almost nothing except noodles.

title: How to Watch a Sumo Tournament Without Watching It on TV
excerpt: Six tournaments a year, three of them in Tokyo. Tickets go on sale months in advance and sell out. Here's how to actually get in.

title: The Onsen Rules Nobody Bothers to Tell You
excerpt: The water is shared. The silence is expected. The tattoo policy is more complicated than you've been told.

title: Don Quijote: What to Buy, What to Skip, and How to Survive the Store
excerpt: Don Quijote is five floors of everything at prices that make no sense. The key is knowing what you came for before you walk in.

title: Hiroshima Is More Than the Peace Park — And the Peace Park Is More Than You Think
excerpt: People visit Hiroshima for one reason. Most leave having found three or four others.

title: Autumn Leaves in Japan: Where to Go and When the Timing Actually Works
excerpt: Koyo — autumn foliage — is not a fixed event. It starts in Hokkaido in September and ends in Kyushu in December. The timing requires a decision.

title: Beppu: The Onsen City That's Stranger and Better Than You Expect
excerpt: Beppu produces more geothermal steam per day than anywhere in Japan and possibly anywhere outside Iceland. The city treats this as completely normal.

title: Japanese Stationery Is Worth the Suitcase Space
excerpt: Pens, notebooks, tape, paper clips. Japan has turned the mundane into an argument for why other countries aren't trying hard enough.

title: Eating at a Sushi Counter: What to Expect and How to Not Ruin It
excerpt: The sushi counter is not intimidating once you understand that there are three rules, they're easy, and the chef wants you to enjoy it.

title: Nara Beyond the Deer: What to Do After the First Hour
excerpt: Yes, the deer are free-roaming and yes, they will bow to get crackers from you. This takes about 40 minutes. Nara has a full day's worth of things after that.

title: Golden Week: What It Is, Why It Will Destroy Your Trip, and When to Go Instead
excerpt: Golden Week runs from late April to early May. If your trip overlaps it — or Obon, or New Year — you have two options: embrace the chaos or reschedule.

title: What to Buy When You Buy Japanese Sake
excerpt: Sake is rice wine in the same way that champagne is grape juice. The category is more complex than most people expect, and the range of quality is enormous.

title: Hokkaido in July: Japan's Best-Kept Summer Secret
excerpt: Tokyo in July is 35 degrees and 90% humidity. Hokkaido in July is 22 degrees and clear. These two facts explain a lot.

title: Koenji and Shimokitazawa: Tokyo for People Who've Already Done Harajuku
excerpt: Two stops on different lines. Two neighborhoods that run on thrift stores, live music, and a specific refusal to be improved.

title: How to Actually Eat Wagyu Beef in Japan
excerpt: Wagyu is expensive. This is not a misunderstanding. The question is what you're getting for the expense, and whether a ¥5,000 lunch version is the same as a ¥30,000 dinner.

title: Japan's Vending Machines Are a Serious Subject
excerpt: There are 4 million vending machines in Japan. One for every 31 people. This is not an accident.

title: Day Trips From Tokyo That Aren't Hakone or Nikko
excerpt: Hakone is excellent. Nikko is impressive. Both are in every guidebook and overrun on weekends. There are better options if you're willing to look slightly further.

title: Omiyage: The Art of Bringing Back the Right Thing
excerpt: Returning from anywhere in Japan without gifts for the people you left behind is not a neutral act. Omiyage culture runs deep, and buying well requires knowing the rules.

title: The Hidden Shrines of Kyoto Locals Still Keep Secret
excerpt: Beyond Fushimi Inari and Kinkaku-ji lies another Kyoto — quiet, moss-covered and usually empty. The city has well over a thousand shrines and temples, and most of them see almost nobody on a weekday morning.

title: How to Spend 10 Days in Japan Without a Single Tourist Trap
excerpt: Most first-time visitors follow the same Golden Route — Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka — and come home feeling like they saw a theme park. This itinerary takes a different approach: slower, deeper, and built around the neighborhoods that locals actually use.

title: The Perfect Route up Mt. Fuji: What Nobody Tells You
excerpt: Climbing Fuji sounds straightforward until you are doing it at 3am in a queue of headlamps. The mountain rewards preparation, punishes assumptions, and is now a permit-and-quota mountain rather than an open one.

title: Osaka in 3 Days: The Eating and Wandering Itinerary
excerpt: Osaka has a reputation as Japan's kitchen and that barely scratches it. A city best travelled by eating your way across it, arranged into three days that still leave room to wander.

title: Yakushima: Japan's Ancient Forest That Few Tourists Find
excerpt: A UNESCO-listed island covered in cedar trees that are older than many civilizations, Yakushima sits off the southern tip of Kyushu and sees a fraction of the visitors it deserves. The hike through Shiratani Unsuikyo inspired Princess Mononoke — and it still feels that way.

title: How to Read a Japanese Menu Without Speaking Japanese
excerpt: Most Japanese restaurants don't have English menus, and that's not a problem once you know what to look for. A handful of kanji, some pattern recognition, and the willingness to point gets you through almost any restaurant in the country.

title: What Wabi-Sabi Really Means — And Why the World Needs It Now
excerpt: The Japanese aesthetic of imperfection and transience offers something Western design philosophy rarely does: permission to be incomplete. Wabi-sabi isn't a style — it's a way of perceiving, and learning to see it changes how you look at almost everything.

title: Kintsugi: The Art of Repairing Broken Things with Gold
excerpt: A 500-year-old technique for mending ceramics with lacquer and powdered gold has become a global metaphor for resilience. The craft itself is slower, stranger and far more demanding than the metaphor suggests.

title: Hanami 2026: Where to See Cherry Blossoms Like a Local
excerpt: Skip the crush at Maruyama Park and Ueno. The good hanami spots follow a pattern — canals, school grounds, old railway embankments — and once you know the pattern you can find them on any map before you leave the hotel.

title: The Best Japanese Kitchen Knives to Bring Home
excerpt: Japanese knives are the single best souvenir you can carry out of Japan — functional, beautiful, and something you'll use every day for decades. This guide covers every price point from a ¥4,000 entry knife to the hand-forged blade worth saving up for.

title: Buying Matcha: Ceremonial vs. Culinary Grade Explained
excerpt: The matcha market is flooded with products that taste nothing like what you drink in a tea ceremony — and the price tag is not a reliable guide. Here's how to read labels, what to taste for, and where to buy the real thing.

title: 10 Japanese Drugstore Products Worth Every Yen
excerpt: Japanese pharmacies are overwhelming in the best way — walls of skincare, hair treatments, and stomach remedies at prices that make no sense until you try them. These are the ten products that actually earn their place in your luggage.

title: Where to Buy Authentic Yukata in Tokyo Without the Markup
excerpt: The tourist-district yukata sold near Asakusa are fine, but the ones sold at department store basements and specialist shops are extraordinary — and often cheaper. This guide takes you past the obvious options to the places worth visiting.

title: The JR Pass in 2026: When It Saves Money and When It Doesn't
excerpt: Since the 2023 price rise the pass stopped being an automatic purchase, and it gets more expensive again in October 2026. The arithmetic is simple, and for most itineraries it now says no.

title: Getting From the Airport Into the City: Narita, Haneda and Kansai
excerpt: Three airports, three completely different problems. The wrong choice at Narita costs two hours and the price of a nice dinner, and the decision is easier to make before you land than after.

title: Send Your Suitcase Ahead: How Takkyubin Changes a Japan Trip
excerpt: Japan has a next-day courier network that will move your suitcase between hotels for the price of a decent lunch. Almost no visitor uses it, and almost every visitor should.

title: Where to Sleep in Japan: Every Accommodation Type, Honestly Compared
excerpt: Business hotel, capsule, ryokan, hostel, minshuku, apartment. They are not points on a price ladder — they are different products, and the cheap one is often the right one.

title: What a Japan Trip Actually Costs, Line by Line
excerpt: Japan has a reputation for being expensive that is thirty years out of date in some categories and entirely accurate in others. Here is where the money really goes.

title: Accessible Travel in Japan: What Works Well and What Still Doesn't
excerpt: Japan's rail network is one of the most accessible in the world, and its older streets and buildings are among the least. Both things are true at once, and planning around the gap is the whole task.

title: Vegetarian, Vegan, Halal and Allergies: Eating in Japan With Restrictions
excerpt: The hard part is not finding restaurants. It is that dashi is in almost everything savoury, and 'no meat' does not communicate that to anyone.

title: Fukuoka: The Japanese City That Gets Everything Right
excerpt: An international airport eleven minutes from the city centre, the best ramen in the country, and street food stalls along the river. Fukuoka is consistently rated the most liveable city in Japan and consistently skipped by visitors.

title: Nagasaki: The Port That Was Japan's Only Window on the World
excerpt: For two centuries, when the country was closed, one artificial island in Nagasaki harbour was the entire point of contact with Europe. The city that grew from that is unlike anywhere else in Japan — and it carries the second atomic bombing.

title: Sendai and Matsushima: The Easiest Way Into Tohoku
excerpt: Ninety minutes north of Tokyo by Shinkansen and almost nobody goes. A green city built around a warlord's legacy, and a bay of pine-covered islands that has been considered one of Japan's three great views for four hundred years.

title: Aomori and Hirosaki: Late Blossom, Big Festivals, Deep Snow
excerpt: At the top of Honshu, the cherry trees flower when Kyoto has finished, the summer festival is the loudest in Japan, and the winter snow is measured in metres. This is the region that rewards going at the wrong time of year.

title: Ginzan Onsen: The Snow Town That Had to Start Turning People Away
excerpt: A single street of wooden inns along a river, lit by gas lamps, buried in snow. It became too photogenic for its own good, and the town now controls who can walk down it in winter.

title: Okinawa: A Different Country That Happens to Be in Japan
excerpt: Subtropical, formerly an independent kingdom, and shaped by the worst battle of the Pacific war and eighty years of American bases since. Okinawa is the part of Japan that is least like the rest of it.

title: The Yaeyama Islands: Closer to Taiwan Than to Tokyo
excerpt: Four hundred kilometres beyond Okinawa's main island lies a group where the jungle reaches the water, the villages have coral walls and sand streets, and the night sky is the darkest in Japan.

title: Okinawan Food: Pork, Bitter Melon and the Longevity Myth
excerpt: Not Japanese food as you know it. Chinese technique, south-east Asian ingredients, American canned pork, and a set of dishes built around a bitter gourd most first-timers approach with suspicion.

title: Hakodate: The Port Town at the Bottom of Hokkaido
excerpt: A morning market selling squid you catch yourself, a hillside of nineteenth-century foreign consulates, and a night view that Japan has been ranking against Hong Kong and Naples for a century.

title: Skiing in Hokkaido: Why the Snow Is Actually Different
excerpt: Siberian air crossing a warm sea produces snow so dry it does not pack. That single meteorological accident is why skiers fly past the Alps to get to an island north of Japan.

title: Okayama and Kurashiki: A Great Garden and a Canal District
excerpt: One of Japan's three great landscape gardens, and half an hour away a merchant quarter of white-walled warehouses along a willow-lined canal that survived the war entirely intact.

title: Izumo and Matsue: The Oldest Shrine and the Quietest Coast
excerpt: On the far side of the mountains from everything else, a shrine that predates written Japanese history, a castle that was never rebuilt because it never burned, and a garden ranked first in the country for two decades.

title: The 88 Temples: Walking the Shikoku Pilgrimage
excerpt: Twelve hundred kilometres, eighty-eight temples and roughly six weeks on foot around an entire island. Most people do a fraction of it, and the fraction still works.

title: Matsuyama and Dogo Onsen: Japan's Oldest Hot Spring
excerpt: A bathhouse mentioned in eighth-century chronicles, a wooden building from 1894 that reopened in 2024 after five and a half years of restoration, and a castle on a hill above both.

title: Buying Japanese Ceramics: Regions, Shapes and Getting Them Home
excerpt: Every region makes pottery and every region's pottery looks different. Knowing four or five of the styles turns a shelf of similar bowls into a choice worth making.

title: Tenugui, Furoshiki and Noren: Japanese Cloth Worth Buying
excerpt: Flat, light, cheap and useful. Japanese textiles are the best souvenirs nobody thinks to buy, and they weigh nothing in a suitcase already full of ceramics.

title: Where to Actually Shop: Department Stores, 100-Yen Shops and the Rest
excerpt: Japanese retail is organised by type of shop rather than by price, and knowing which kind of building to walk into saves more money and time than any list of individual stores.

title: Bowing: What It Actually Means and What Visitors Should Do
excerpt: You will be bowed to several hundred times a day and you are not expected to return most of them. The rules are simpler than they look, and getting them slightly wrong is entirely fine.

title: The Little Tray: How Paying for Things Works in Japan
excerpt: There is a small dish beside every till and it is not decorative. Money is placed, not handed, and the change comes back with a precision that visitors mistake for suspicion.

title: Japanese Toilets: The Control Panel, and Where to Find One
excerpt: Heated seats, a panel of unlabelled buttons, and public facilities that are free, everywhere and clean. The toilets are one of the things visitors talk about most and prepare for least.
